notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1206.tmp1206.opp-lat: The Virgil quotations are Georgics 4.248–9 and Aeneid 1.76–7. In §1 'Hoc in te proprie exempli lucentibus' is corrupt; translated as if 'propriis exemplis lucentibus' ('by your own shining examples'). 'Servato tenore ... Ecclesiae' is taken as keeping to the wording of the church's [Marmoutier's] copy; the page number '1271' has been left out. In §1 the subjects of the siege narrative are ambiguous in the Latin; they are interpreted here as Maximian besieging Florus. 'De die in diem' is restored from the garbled 'diem'. Other corrections of evident scanning errors: 'juribus' read as 'jussibus' (commands); 'matis' as 'matris'; 'imiendere' as 'impendere'; 'contemptari ... coaetur' as 'contemplari ... cogatur'. The bracket after 'transcendat' is the editor's note that the syntax requires 'transcendisse'; it is translated as such. The edition's square brackets marking interpolated passages are kept. 'Cucusam' is taken to be Cucusus in Cappadocia.

Line 5: 'Aumari' among the great-uncles is taken as Amnarus, the brother of the elder Florus named earlier. 'Patruelis' and 'consobrinos' are rendered 'cousin(s)', although by the work's own genealogy the seven are sons of Martin's paternal uncles. Line 6: 'Gualberrum' is read as Gualbertus, following the next section; 'Condatensem vicum' is taken as Candes.

Line 7: 'vixerunt cum eo ... annis sexdecim' rendered as written. 'Permalimas' read as 'Permaluimus' (we preferred); the syntax of that sentence is loose and rendered as closely as possible. 'In Codice l'atrictacensi, de Percy' is garbled; probably 'Patriciacensi' (Percy); rendered as the Percy codex. Final antiphon: 'Avcte' read as 'Auctae'/'Sancti' uncertain; 'juinti dicastis' read as 'juncti dicastis' (together you dedicated); first word possibly a vocative epithet now corrupt.

nodes.text: HISTORY OF THE SEVEN SLEEPERS.
LETTER OF SAINT GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, TO THE BLESSED SULPICIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, ON THE LIFE OF THE SEVEN HOLY SLEEPERS.
To the most blessed father Sulpicius, by the grace of God archbishop of Bourges, Gregory, unworthy priest of Tours, [wishes] everlasting salvation in God our Saviour.

In the poet, the virtue and prudence of the saints is praised under the figure of bees, when he says: "The more they have been drained, the more keenly do they all set themselves to repair the ruins of their fallen race" (Virgil, Georgics 4). This, most blessed Father, I may be permitted to have set at the head of my letter, as I consider with how much prudence and how much care you strive to make firm the state of the tottering Church and to repair its ruins. This you do not cease to do by your own shining examples, by the honeyed words of exhorting sermons, and finally by bringing the deeds of the saints who went before into public view. This is why, among the other things that your Highness has commanded of my littleness (for a friend's admonition is indeed a pressing command), [you asked] that I should commit to writing the deeds, life and end of the Seven Sleepers, who are said to rest at the monastery of Marmoutier and whose very renowned fame is spread far and wide, if I could find them anywhere. Then I, after my custom and out of reverence for you, answered in the words of the poet: "Yours, kind father, is the task of setting out what you desire; mine it is right to carry out what I am bidden" (Virgil, Aeneid 1). And at once, following your command with the foot of obedience close behind, as they say, I searched the book-chests of the churches and turned over the libraries, and at last at the aforesaid monastery of Marmoutier I found what I was seeking. Keeping, therefore, to the wording of that church, I have sent a transcript to your Paternity, as you had asked. For the rest, it is yours to make it known, and yours, for the grace of Christ, to seek out, to build churches, and to obtain the grace of Christ the Lord for your friend, or rather your obedient servant.

HERE BEGINS THE LIFE, OR CONDUCT, AND ALSO THE DEATH, OF THE SEVEN HOLY SLEEPERS, WHOSE BODIES ARE KEPT IN MARMOUTIER, AND WHOSE NAMES ARE WRITTEN HERE: CLEMENS, PRIMUS, LAETUS, THEODORUS, GAUDENS, QUIRIACUS, INNOCENTIUS.

1. In the times of Diocletian and Maximian, as their cruelty drove it, almost the whole world began to fall away and withdraw from the power of the Romans; and among many others the kingdom of the Huns withdrew, under the rule of Florus, a most vigorous king. This Florus obtained the kingdom when he was twenty years old, his father, named Amnarus, having lately gone the way of all flesh. This same Florus had two brothers younger than himself, Martin and Amnarus. The aforesaid Florus took as wife a most beautiful girl named Brichildis, daughter of Chut, king of the Saxons, by whom he begot three sons: the firstborn Florus, father of blessed Martin of Tours; the second Hilgrinus; the third Amnarus. The second, Hilgrinus, begot four sons, Clemens, Primus, Laetus and Theodorus. The third, Amnarus, begot three, Gaudens, Quiriacus and Innocentius. When Florus, then, had held his kingdom happily for about ten years, he was attacked by Maximian. He, toiling for about three years, barely and with the greatest difficulty entered the first parts of his kingdom, and not without the death and bloodshed of his fighters. For Florus, clashing with him two and three times, had put him to flight in shameful defeat. But through the treachery of [Florus's] own men he seized a certain fortress and fortified it against him and his kingdom; and so a second and a third. At last he besieged him in a very strongly fortified fortress with almost the whole nobility of the Huns. Besieged for half a year, [Florus] was compelled to come to surrender, life and limb being granted to him and his men. And [Maximian] led the captives with him to Rome, among whom were the two brothers of King Florus, Martin and Amnarus. [Florus] had not yet begotten sons, except his firstborn, namely Florus, three years old; the other two he begot after his return from captivity. When they had been presented to Diocletian, he sent them to prison. After about half a year, Diocletian, remembering the prowess of Florus, ordered him to be presented to him. Seeing that his beauty had withered through the filth and hardship of prison, he was moved with pity; and he released him and sent him back to his own, allowing him his kingdom with its revenues for his lifetime, the fortifications being taken away or seized [Ed., broken]. He allowed him to reign on such terms that after his death his son should not be raised to the kingship, nor to the consulship, but should be only a tribune. When this had been confirmed on both sides, he withdrew with all his men.

II. Having returned, in the same year he begot two twin sons, Hilgrinus and Amnarus. [But God, who does not accept the person of princes and rejects their counsels, who hardens whom he will and gives them up to a reprobate mind and brings them to stupor, allowed even the emperors who had long harried the Church with most grievous persecutions to come to so great a change of madness and vanity that Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan, on one day laying aside the insignia of empire, lived after their rule as private men, like commoners. But Maximian, repenting of the deed not long after, when he had laid an ambush and was plotting the death of his son-in-law Constantine, who now held the realm, was caught at Marseilles when his trickery was detected, and not long after, in prison, his neck broken by a noose, he was strangled; or, as some assert, suffocated by demons, he ended his impious life with a fitting death. Diocletian too, understanding that for the same reason he had become suspect to the same Constantine, drank poison and became the impious punisher of himself, and in his villa near the town of Salona closed the last day of his life. These having thus been punished with both temporal and eternal death, when after the foul and dreadful darkness of wars and persecutions the long-desired calm of peace began by divine will to shine widely throughout the world,] Florus handed over his firstborn Florus to be brought up by Constantine, who had succeeded those same emperors, Diocletian and Maximian, after a very short time, with only his father Constantius and Galerius Maximian coming between together; and this same Constantine always held him dear and beloved. And when he had grown up and been made a soldier, he gave him as wife his niece, the daughter of his sister, and having appointed him tribune sent him back to his father. He, by this same wife, while his father was still living, begot a son, whom he ordered to be called Florus. He [was indeed born in the seventeenth year of Constantine, but] afterwards, in the time of [his son] Constantius, by God's disposing, he was made a catechumen and baptised by blessed Paul, bishop of Constantinople, and was called Martin. [His venerable baptiser, the same patriarch Paul, was driven into exile for the Catholic faith by that same Constantius, who on succeeding his father in the empire had turned aside into the Arian heresy, to a certain small town of Cappadocia named Cucusus, and was there cruelly strangled by the plots of the Arians, and passed as victor to the heavenly kingdom.] The elder Florus, worn out with old age, closed his last day; he left his land to his firstborn and left his two young brothers in his hands. He, after his father's death, ruled the land manfully, and joined his brothers in marriage with daughters of the noblest men of the district of the Huns, from whom his firstborn, namely Hilgrinus, as was said before, begot four sons, and the second, Amnarus, three.

III. Florus the tribune, then, son of King Florus, when Constantine had died and Constantius was reigning, came to Constantinople with his little son Florus, whom he commended to the emperor, who kept him with him and made him a soldier. [Him too, while still a youth, Julian Caesar, when he was sent by this same Constantius, his cousin, into Gaul against the barbarians who were harassing the lands of the Romans, not knowing what [Constantius] was planning concerning him, took with him to bring aid, and kept him in his retinue to be trained in soldiering as long as he had power.] But the holy man chose rather to serve the heavenly God than to fight under an earthly emperor. [For he was made especially for this: that the triumphal banner of the holy cross should be carried into the western parts of the world to be raised and adored, and that he should exchange the oaths of soldiering for the commands of the Gospel. He, famous for his ancestors but more famous for his merits, holy from infancy, devout from boyhood, advancing day by day from virtue to virtue, shone in the world with great miracles and was resplendent far and wide with Catholic teaching. For he who had begun at the outset of the ways of God with such great virtue and so great and astonishing a miracle, what wonder if he always had prosperous courses and blessed outcomes in them? Rather, it would be a wonder if, after so wonderful a conversion by which God drew him to himself, he had not continually led, right to the end of his life, a manner of life lofty in the height of its virtues, glorious in the brightness of its miracles, and splendid in the beauty of its religion. For who would not reckon it more wonderful than almost any virtue and miracle that a little child scarcely ten years old should have shuddered at the superstition of pagan error that he had drunk in, so to speak, from the breast with his mother's milk, and, while his parents, guardians and stewards pressed upon him to dissuade him, now with threats, now with blows, now with blandishments, should have fled to the faith of Christ and to the fellowship of the Church, whose sacraments he had not yet received? Who would not extol with the highest praises a boy of twelve who, like a sensible and brave man, disregarding his mother's tenderness, desired the squalor of the desert, and whatever he might have to endure there, as if it were delights; and who, what he could not yet do for the weakness of his body but would later fulfil, already did at least by meditating and desiring it in the sight of God, who sometimes counts the will as the deed? Who would not judge worthy of signal praise a youth brought up in the greatest luxury, entangled in secular soldiering by his father's commands, who, showing himself as a solitary or a monk, kept himself not only from evil works but also from every wicked desire, and preserved himself unharmed in the midst of the Babylonian furnace seething with sulphur and pitch; who, among others plundering what belonged to others and mocking him, gave to the poor not only his superfluities but even his necessities, and indeed went beyond [transcendisse, "went beyond", the syntax requires] the precepts too, as is plain from his dividing his cloak? For we have a precept about giving away one of two garments for Christ, not about dividing one, which this man did, whose heart was ready to spend both his goods and himself for Christ, and for his brothers for Christ's sake. In him, who would not also receive with astonishment this: that, placed among most wealthy and renowned parents, as born of royal ancestors, and compelled to follow the retinue of King Constantius and of Julian Caesar, now of the one, now of the other, in different parts of the world, and in his youth to attach himself to them and serve them as the sons of his maternal uncles, one of whom was an Arian and the other an apostate, both persecutors of the orthodox, in so great a conflict of things opposed to him he both kept his faith uncorrupted, and always embraced earthly poverty, and held to perfect humility! Who would pass over unconsidered this too in him: that, seeing Christ clothed with that part of the cloak with which he had covered the poor man, and as it were displaying it and glorying in it before the angels, he did not glory in so great and so glorious a vision, in which another would have gloried, but was rather humbled, and with panting desire, like a thirsting hart for the springs of waters, having returned to Constantinople and received the sacrament of baptism from blessed Paul, patriarch of that city, as we said before, he resolved to bring gladly to fulfilment what he had been earnestly turning over in his breast, what he had long laboured to bring forth in his fervour, and what now, as if come to birth by natural ripeness, was eager to burst out into the fruit of life? What was this? Namely, that, trampling on all the delights of the enticing world, he might be free for God, and, raising up a heavenly manner of life without interruption from outward care, might taste more often and see how sweet the Lord is. Though he reckoned this one thing most necessary, according to the Lord's saying, and burned vehemently to attain this alone, who would not delight to contemplate, who would not be compelled to imitate, with what simple and sincere charity he put it off for his brother's salvation? O truly wonderful kindness of the holy youth! For though he knew that he could obtain this best part, which is taken from no one who attains it, only in the cleft of the rock and the hollow of the wall, where there is the one protection and singular refreshment for those who flee into a shade by day from the heat, and into security and hiding from the whirlwind and the rain, yet out of his wish to save his comrade, against his own wish, he endured the evils of the world for two years, standing outside as if without a roof among storms, rain-clouds and hail, in the mire of the deep, on the slippery ground of the world, where his foot could find no rest; where he was not only afflicted with injuries but also pressed by countless dangers. What would he do, or rather what would he not do, for the salvation of many, who for the devotion of one endured so much weariness and bore so long a loss of his own quiet? What crosses, what tortures, what injuries, if they were inflicted for the Saviour's sake, would he not prefer to all banquets however delicate, who for love of a mortal man so long put off fulfilling the one equal desire of his singular joy, by whose delay he was sharply tormented? But surely the holy young man's patience was being exercised, his fortitude tested, his experience formed, and he was learning beforehand in himself, by spontaneous charity, what later, at the fitting time, when he was set as bishop of souls, he would have to do with due care concerning many. So taught from youth, he did this very thing in old age, beyond almost all men, and more than ought to have been required of him: in the days of the emperor Maximus, when, walking according to the charity that does not seek its own, he not only wished to become, as Paul [did], but almost made himself, anathema from Christ for the brothers of a guilty communion, entering into their assembly not by will but by necessity, so that he might take thought for the churches of Spain, over whose necks the sword of the savage king was hanging. But knowing without doubt that to fulfil the law the burdens of some must be borne by others, knowing that love is the fullness of the law, knowing that charity is the bond of perfection and the beginning of the spiritual fruits; knowing that through it we must serve one another, that it never fails, and that one who walks in it does not stray or falter, relying on the support of so great a virtue he confidently presumed that whatever loss he might at any time incur for its preservation could very easily be restored or made good through that charity which covers a multitude of sins. And I beg that this digression, made out of admiration and to contemplate the merits of Martin while still of youthful age, may not be burdensome to anyone nor judged idle, since the sum of this whole little work looks to him, and since we have moved our stylus, sluggish though it be, no less to show both the abundance of his charity, with which he always wholly overflowed, and the nobility of his origin, passed over by Severus, the first writer of his Life, than to make known to posterity the venerable manner of life and the death of his aforesaid kinsmen.

IV. But to return now from these matters to the course of the narrative we have undertaken: Martin, having put off the old man and put on the new through baptism, was won over by the entreaty of his tribune, whom he was striving so hard to gain for Christ, and who promised that when the term of his tribuneship had run out he would serve God, changed in life and habit; and, bound as it were by affection, he remained in the retinue for two years, applying himself not to plunder but, as he had begun, to holy works. When this waiting, which he bore most heavily, was over, he did not rest at once, but renounced flesh and blood; and, though Caesar resisted and was indignant, he forswore worldly military service and gave up his parents, his estates and the homeland in which he was born and known, in which he was rich and renowned, and could for that reason have been held revered and magnificent. God destining him to be our patron, he fled into these foreign regions, where he would be reckoned unknown and without glory, an exile and a praiseworthy poor man, as proof of his great humility. There he submitted himself to be taught by the teaching and example of the most excellent and distinguished man Hilary, who in those days appeared as the singular lamp and pillar of the Gallican Church. He became his disciple so that he should not run in vain or dangerously, if he were carried along by his own judgement and made himself his own master, and so that he should not fall into the number of those to whom it is said: Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own sight (Isa. 5:21). When, as he toiled in the school of virtues, he was ordered by his master to ascend to the higher grade of the Levitical order, he himself, for the increase of his progress, settled in the lowest office, that of exorcist, the more securely the more humbly, his master at last granting it and marvelling. What then was to become of this man, founded on such great humility? Was it not that, according to the Scriptures, glory should receive the humble in spirit, and that he who had humbled himself should be exalted by the supreme teacher of humility, whom he was so nearly following; and that, powerful in deed and word and worthy of the apostolic ministry, he should make known to others the ways of life which he had searched out in silence as a subordinate? But how should he come to the ministry unless he were taken up? And how should he preach unless he were sent? Therefore, while he was living in the utmost subjection with his master and being instructed in quiet, thinking nothing great of himself and planning nothing lofty, he was ordered through a revelation by the Lord, who looked upon the heart of his little one and valued it highly, to do the work of an evangelist, and was admonished to visit his parents, whom the error of paganism still held bound, in order to impart to them the faith of Christ. Relying therefore on the divine oracle, with the leave of blessed Hilary (for he had not yet been sent into exile by the Augustus Constantius for the defence of the faith), he set out devoutly whither he had been ordered; and, spreading the word of God all around, he strove to bring a great harvest into the barn of Christ from the conversion of unbelievers, and, with heavenly grace working with him, he converted his parents to the profession of the Christian faith, only his father, by the inscrutable judgement of God, remaining in the image and error of the earthly man, and defending the superstition of fanatical worship solely on the authority of old usage, wrongly imbibed from infancy. His mother too, who had borne him for the world, he himself regenerated in Christ, becoming the spiritual father of her whose carnal son he was, and granting her to be in some sense the beginning of a new creature for the world, from whom he himself, after God, had received the beginning of his existence as a man. And he brought it about that both she and the others whom he had won for salvation were reborn in Christ at the hands of his father's paternal uncles, that is, his own great-uncles Martin and Amnarus, who were most Christian and held the office of bishop in the cities assigned to them; among those baptised were also his uncles Hilgrinus and Amnarus, with their seven sons, namely Clement, Primus, Laetus and Theodore, Gaudens, Quiriacus and Innocent. Their fathers, Hilgrinus and Amnarus, did not divide their paternal inheritance as other brothers do, but, just as they had been born twins of one birth, so they were content with one house, one estate and one common property, with their wives and sons. In the same year in which they were baptised they entered the way of all flesh. So their seven sons named above, selling all their estates, distributed the price to the poor and made their slaves free. They themselves shut themselves up in a certain place, devoting themselves to reading, prayer and psalmody, content with only two young servants, who rendered them the service of comfort. They lived settled in an upper room without complaint, pleasing both to God and to men, lacking the pleasant company of wives and children, and striving to lead a celibate life. Of the leftovers of their food, wherever they were carried, by whatever sick people they were taken, and whatever sickness these were held by, they were at once healed. For this reason almost everyone, coming first from the neighbouring province and afterwards from that whole region, venerated them as prophets of God. Of these many, imitating their faith through their preaching, submitted to Christianity, and, putting off the old man, put on the new, who is created according to God. In short, all venerated them with services and many gifts. Moreover princes, tribunes and soldiers, Christians, Jews and pagans visited them, revered them and honoured them. Disturbed by this, the servants of God, fearing to become subject to vainglory and the ambition of this world, and seeking the refuge of flight, resolved to leave their homeland: for in this they had as an example Abraham, and more recently many other righteous men, and most recently their cousin, the most blessed Martin. [He, as one who obediently heard both the precepts and the counsels of Christ, had put nothing before His love, but, leaving all things, taking up the cross and denying himself, following Him as leader and committing himself to His judgement, had cast away the freedom of his own will, which is ruinous to all; so Christ too, generously fulfilling in him the sentence of His promise, had made him illustrious, although he fled from these things, with the glory of miracles, the honour of the episcopate and an abundance of riches, and had already here repaid him the hundredfold promised to His followers, keeping for him in the future the fullness of an unending reward. And when he had gone out alone from his land and his kindred for Christ's sake, the same Christ his leader magnifying him in the land of his sojourning and working wonders at the word of his mouth, wonderful to say, he raised up children to Abraham from stones, and changed the hearts of men, and led the erring and unbelieving to the paths of righteousness and the prudence of the just. He overthrew shrines, founded monasteries, built churches; and so, growing little by little, he had become a great nation.]

V. So the aforesaid, hearing the fame of his holiness and the renown of his name, and that he had been appointed to the bishopric of the city of Tours, took counsel, and with small provision and scanty baggage gathered, determined to go all the way to him and to live by his counsel; and so it was done. Coming to the city of Tours, they found blessed Martin in his bishopric, celebrating, as was his custom, the solemnities of Mass on the Lord's day, and they asked for a blessing in the manner of pilgrims. When the divine solemnities of Mass were finished [Al., performed], the most blessed Martin recognised them as his kinsmen and cousins; and he wept over each of them and kissed them; and taking them with him across the river, where a multitude of brothers dwelt, he invited them to a meal in common with the brothers. On the following day they recounted the whole course of their pilgrimage, saying that their wish was to visit the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, and also to go on to Jerusalem to visit the Lord's tomb and to adore the Lord's cross, and to come by way of the tomb of blessed James, and so to return to him. Setting out on this journey with blessed Martin's blessing, barefoot, wearing woollen clothes, content with bread and water and raw herbs, they completed it in five years. Returning safe and sound, they presented themselves to blessed Martin with many relics, namely from the Lord's tomb and His most holy cross, also from the tomb of holy Mary, mother of the Lord, and from her garments, from the relics of the apostles Peter and Paul and of St James, brother of the Lord, and from many others; blessed Martin received these reverently and placed them with reverence in the apse of the greater church. The seven brothers themselves, giving themselves up to blessed Martin and to the brothers dwelling there, both in soul and in body, vowed that they would not depart from that place. Blessed Martin at once received them gladly, clothed them in the monastic habit and confirmed them with his own blessing; and he placed them in a cave in the side of a hollowed hill, and also made them an oratory in the rock itself, and blessed an altar, where with his own hand he also laid up the relics which they had brought. He ordained Clement and Primus priests, Laetus and Theodore deacons, Gaudens, Quiriacus and Innocent subdeacons. They remained in that cell or oratory, where they delighted in fasting, prayer, silence and reading, as long as blessed Martin survived. He, foreknowing his death long beforehand through a revelation, arranged to go to the village of Candes, to restore peace among the clergy of that church, who were at odds; and knowing also through the Spirit that he would not return, he called together all the brothers of the monastery, kissed and blessed each one, and set over them in his place one of the brothers, named Gualbertus, appointed him abbot and confirmed him with his blessing; and to him he commended the seven aforesaid brothers, his cousins, and he, receiving them in common with the other brothers, loved them especially, and visited and strengthened them spiritually.

VI. Blessed Martin, after his death, until the day of their departure, very often appeared to them in a vision, consoling and strengthening them. They lived with him in their holy way of life for sixteen years, and after his passing twenty-five: that is, under Gualbertus the first abbot for twenty-three years, and under Aicardus the second abbot for two years. In the time of this Aicardus, the second abbot, it happened that the feast of the passing of blessed Martin fell on a Saturday; and on the following day, on which we celebrate the Lord's Day, after the solemnities of matins were completed, at midnight blessed Martin appeared to them, announcing to them the day of their death, and saying: 'Tomorrow, very early in the morning, call Abbot Aicardus here to you; and when he stands by, let each of you make known to him the whole course of your life and your deeds, confessing all your sins. Tell him also from me to celebrate a mass in honour of the Holy Trinity, making commemoration of me and of the saints whose relics are contained in the present altar consecrated by me, and to set out a separate host to be offered for each one of you [another reading: to be offered up]; and when these are consecrated, each of you will receive communion. When communion is completed, and you have received the viaticum of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the mass is ended, you will prostrate yourselves in prayer and enter on the way of all flesh, as free from the pain of death as you are strangers to the corruption of the flesh; and so you will be received by angels and led upward by me myself, until we present you before the tribunal of Christ.' All of this was done as blessed Martin commanded. When they had received communion [another reading: the viaticum] from the hand of Abbot Aicardus, and the mass was ended, on bended knees, sound and unharmed, prostrate in prayer, they entered on the way of all flesh, as blessed Martin had foretold, as free from the pain of death as they had been strangers to the corruption of the flesh. At once that cell was filled with so great a fragrance that one would have thought a heap of many spices had been scattered there. Abbot Aicardus, together with the brothers, taking them up not as from death but as from prayer, did not think them dead but sleeping, since their faces were ruddy like a rose and their flesh shone like snow. For this reason he arranged them on seats, as they had been accustomed to sit in their cell, and placed them so that they could be seen by all, with only what was needed to protect them from harm by those rushing in, namely barriers of bars set between them and those entering. The doors also stood open, so that all who came might see the faces of the saints, not as of the dead but as of the sleeping: for although they were dead to men, yet to God, for whom all things live, they were sleeping. For the seven days during which they remained above ground that most sweet fragrance did not fail. So great was the multitude of those coming that it filled as much as the place could admit or the roads and paths could hold. All those sick with fever or chills who came returned healthy; and many lepers, deaf, dumb and lame were cured. Those who could not come were carried on beds and pallets, and from the sweetness of the fragrance they returned well. At last, on the seventh day after their passing, Abbot Aicardus, having gathered the brothers of the holy monastery, attended the funeral. He also sent for and summoned the most holy old man, the bishop of the see of the city of Tours, blessed Brice, together with clergy and people; and having taken counsel, they buried them, clothed as they were, in that very cell or oratory, before the altar of that oratory, which had been consecrated by blessed Martin with the relics of the saints. They passed away on the day before the Ides of November, the second day after the feast on which the passing of Saint Martin is celebrated, and they were laid to rest on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December. Buried in the earth, they show that they live in Christ by works of power and miracles, through the grace of the same Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.
Here ends the life and death of the Seven Sleepers.
HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF BLESSED GREGORY, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS, TO THE LIFE OF BLESSED MAURILIUS, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR.
(From several manuscripts.)

To the most holy lord Germanus, bishop of the holy mother Church of Paris, Gregory, humble bishop of the metropolis of Tours, greeting. You have asked that the Lives and miracles which the Lord deigned to work through blessed Maurilius and Albinus, bishops of Angers, which the priest Fortunatus had written down in brilliant language, but which are now almost corrupted by the faults of copyists, we should correct with the skill of our authority and send to your Devotion, who desire to profit from the examples of those before you. But recalling that, if we do this, we shall be torn by the barking and bites of the faithless, who know not how to seek learning but only to envy, we are shaken by the grief of a twofold weariness, since we fear both not to obey your commands and to displease those very people. Yet trusting in the promises of the Almighty, who, speaking through his prophet, made known that those who sow in tears shall reap in joy (Ps. 125:6), I shall satisfy your wish. For we know that if anyone sets down in writing, and corrects even in a rustic style, the Lives and works of power of the most holy confessors of Christ, which are worthy of imitation and can profit another age, he will bring both a reward to himself and salvation to those who wish to imitate them. We therefore preferred, holding it a crime not to speak of, or to correct, the works of power of the most precious confessors of Christ Maurilius and Albinus, since they are worthy of memory, using a plebeian pen, as you requested, so that they may rather profit common people, to correct a few things out of very many, yet, as God is witness, most true, omitting very many things published by Fortunatus which might perhaps seem incredible to unbelievers. What we have corrected we have thought more worthily offered to the petition of your Holiness, so that you, who rejoice to imitate them, may profit, formed by their virtues.
HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF SAINT MAURILIUS.

So Maurilius was a native of the town of Milan, born of most distinguished parents, etc. (In the Percy codex in Burgundy, written about eight hundred years ago, after the Life of Saint Albinus, which is usually attributed to Fortunatus, there is this closing formula: Here ends the Life of blessed Albinus, composed by blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Tours.)
ANTIPHON OF SAINT GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, ON SAINTS MEDARD AND GILDARD, BISHOPS AND BROTHERS.
(From a manuscript codex, in Surius under 8 June.)

Holy bishops, great throughout the whole world, twins by birth, equal in holiness, consecrated together, crowned alike, together you have hallowed a feast day: by your merits, Saint Medard, with the renowned Gildard, always bring help to the people who ask.
